questions.question: The primary goal of fiscal policy reforms post-1991 was to ____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Reduce fiscal deficit and inflation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **fiscal policy reforms** introduced after **1991** were a response to the severe **economic crisis** characterized by a high **fiscal deficit** and a **balance of payments** crisis. The primary goal was to bring stability to the macroeconomy by reducing the **fiscal deficit** from **8.4%** of **GDP** in **1990-91** to more sustainable levels. ***Hence, the statement regarding reducing the fiscal deficit is correct.***
 
• Another major objective was to control **inflation**, which had reached double digits, peaking at nearly **17%** in **August 1991**. By tightening the **fiscal policy** and reducing **monetized deficits**, the government aimed to stabilize prices. ***Hence, the statement regarding reducing inflation is correct.***
 
• The reforms focused on **expenditure management**, which involved cutting down on **non-developmental expenditures** and **subsidies**, such as those on fertilizers and exports, to improve the quality of **public spending**.
 
• **Revenue mobilization** was targeted through **tax reforms**. Based on the **Raja Chelliah Committee (1991)**, the government aimed to simplify the tax structure, reduce high tax rates, and broaden the **tax base** to ensure better compliance.
 
• The reforms also aimed at reducing the **public debt** burden. By **1991**, India’s **internal and external debt** had reached alarming proportions, and fiscal discipline was necessary to avoid a **sovereign default**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **New Economic Policy (NEP) 1991**: Launched under **Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao** and **Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh**, the policy moved the **country** away from a **command economy** toward a **market-oriented economy** through **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG)**.
 
• **Tax Reform Milestones**: Post-**1991**, **Direct Tax** rates (Income and Corporate tax) were significantly lowered. For **example**, the maximum marginal rate of **Personal Income Tax** was reduced to **30%** over time to prevent **tax evasion**.
 
• **Disinvestment**: The government started the process of **disinvestment** in **Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)** to raise **capital** and reduce the **fiscal burden** caused by loss-making state enterprises.
 
• **Monetary Policy Linkage**: The reforms sought to end the **automatic monetization** of the **fiscal deficit** by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** through **Ad-hoc Treasury Bills**, giving the **RBI** more autonomy in **inflation targeting**.
 
• **Trade Policy Reforms**: Fiscal reforms were accompanied by **trade liberalization**, which included the reduction of **import tariffs** and the abolition of **import licensing** for most goods, helping **India** integrate with the **global market**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **FRBM Act, 2003**: A significant development in **India’s** fiscal history was the **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act**, which provided a **legal framework** for the **Central Government** to ensure long-term **macro-economic stability** by setting targets for **fiscal deficit** and **revenue deficit**.
 
• **Subsidies**: Despite reforms, **subsidies** on **food, fertilizer, and petroleum** continue to be a major component of **India’s** fiscal expenditure, often discussed in current **economic surveys** for better **targeting** through **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)**.
 
• **GST Implementation**: The introduction of the **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** on **1st July 2017** is considered the biggest **indirect tax reform** post-**1991**, aiming to create a **unified national market** and improve **revenue collection**.
 
• **Debt-to-GDP Ratio**: Following the **1991** reforms, monitoring the **Debt-to-GDP ratio** became critical to ensuring **fiscal sustainability**, especially during **global financial crises** or **pandemics**.

questions.question: If 2820 is divided into two parts such that one-fifth of the first part and one-eighth of the second part are in the ratio 3 : 4, what is the ratio of the first part to the second part?

Let parts = A and B

(A/5) : (B/8) = 3 : 4

⇒ (A×8)/(B×5) = 3/4

⇒ 32A = 15B

⇒ A : B = 15 : 32

**∴ Answer = 15 : 32**

Total = 2820

Ratio property: a/b = c/d ⇒ ad = bc

⇒ (A/5) : (B/8) = 3 : 4

⇒ (A/5) ÷ (B/8) = 3/4

⇒ (A×8)/(5B) = 3/4

⇒ Cross multiply: 32A = 15B

⇒ A/B = 15/32

⇒ A : B = 15 : 32

questions.question: The period of southwest monsoon season in India is:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**June to September**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Southwest Monsoon** season is the principal rainy season in **India**, traditionally lasting from **June to September**. During this period, the country receives more than **75%** of its total annual rainfall.
 
• The monsoon typically arrives at the **Kerala coast** by **June 1st**. This phenomenon is known as the "burst" of the monsoon, characterized by a sudden increase in rainfall accompanied by thunder and lightning.
 
• The season is divided into two main branches: the **Arabian Sea Branch** and the **Bay of Bengal Branch**. The Arabian Sea branch strikes the **Western Ghats**, while the Bay of Bengal branch moves towards **Northeast India** and the **Indo-Gangetic plains**.
 
• By the middle of **July**, the southwest monsoon covers almost the entire **Indian subcontinent**, providing much-needed relief from the intense summer heat.
 
• The withdrawal of the monsoon begins from **Northwest India** in early **September** and completely exits the northern part of the country by **October**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mechanism of Monsoon:** The monsoon is driven by the differential heating and cooling of **land and water**. During summer, the **Indian landmass** heats up faster than the surrounding oceans, creating a **low-pressure area** over Central India and the **Thar Desert**, which pulls moisture-laden winds from the **Indian Ocean**.
 
• **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ):** The shift of the **ITCZ** to the north over the **Ganga plain** during the summer is a crucial factor in the onset of the southwest monsoon.
 
• **Economic Significance:** The southwest monsoon is the lifeline of the **Indian economy**, as it directly impacts **Kharif crops** like **Rice**, **Maize**, **Cotton**, and **Soybean**. A good monsoon ensures food security and boosts **GDP** growth.
 
• **Geographical Distribution:** Heavy rainfall is recorded in the **Western Ghats** and the **Northeastern states**. For instance, **Mawsynram** and **Cherrapunji** in **Meghalaya** receive the highest rainfall in the world due to the funneling effect of the hills.
 
• **Rain-shadow Areas:** While the windward side of the **Western Ghats** receives heavy rain, the leeward side (the **Deccan Plateau**) remains relatively dry, forming a **rain-shadow area**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **El Niño and La Niña:** These global climatic phenomena significantly influence the Indian monsoon. **El Niño** is generally associated with **droughts** or below-normal rainfall, whereas **La Niña** often brings **excessive rainfall** and flooding.
 
• **Northeast Monsoon:** Following the southwest monsoon, the **Retreating Monsoon** or Northeast Monsoon occurs from **October to December**. This season primarily brings rainfall to the **Coromandel Coast**, specifically states like **Tamil Nadu** and **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• **Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD):** Also known as the "Indian Niño," the **IOD** involves an irregular oscillation of sea-surface temperatures in the western and eastern **Indian Ocean**. A **Positive IOD** often helps in bringing better monsoon rains to **India**, even during an El Niño year.
 
• **Varying Onset Dates:** While **June 1st** is the normal date for Kerala, the onset can vary by a few days each year based on atmospheric conditions and the **Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO)**.

questions.question: Rathwa Ni Gher' is a tribal dance of the Rathwa tribal community of ______________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gujarat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rathwa Ni Gher** is a vibrant folk dance performed by the **Rathwa** tribe, primarily residing in the hilly areas of **Chhota Udepur**, **Vadodara**, and **Panchmahal** districts of **Gujarat**.
 
• The dance is traditionally performed during the festival of **Holi**, which is celebrated by the community as **Gher**. The festivities begin after the **Holika Dahan** and continue for five days.
 
• The performance is a ritualistic offering to **Pithora Dev**, who is the supreme deity of the Rathwas, and it is also linked to the celebration of the **harvest season**.
 
• During the dance, the participants, mostly **men**, wear distinctive costumes that include long **ghaghris** (skirts), **turbans** decorated with **peacock feathers**, and belts with **cowrie shells**.
 
• The rhythm of the dance is maintained by traditional musical instruments like the **Dhol** (drum), **Thali** (brass plate), and **Shehnai**, creating an energetic and rhythmic atmosphere.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tribal Heritage of Gujarat:**

 
 
• **Gujarat** is home to diverse tribal communities like the **Bhils**, **Nayakas**, and **Dhadias**. The state is famous for tribal art forms like the **Siddi Dhamal** dance (associated with **African** descendants) and **Dangi** dances.
 
• The **Rathwa** community is particularly famous for **Pithora Paintings**, which are sacred mural paintings done on the walls of houses to seek protection and prosperity.
 
 
 
• **Geographic and Cultural Context:**
 
 
• The **Rathwa** tribe is one of the largest tribal groups in **Gujarat**. Their culture is deeply rooted in **agriculture** and **animism**, worshipping nature and forest deities.
 
• In contrast, **Kerala** is known for the **Theyyam** and **Thullal** dances; **Tripura** is famous for the **Hojagiri** dance of the **Reang** tribe; and **Himachal Pradesh** is well-known for the **Nati** folk dance.
 
 
 
• **The Kawant Fair:**
 
 
• One of the biggest gatherings for the Rathwas is the **Kawant Mela**, held in the **Chhota Udepur** district. This fair, held a few days after **Holi**, is the primary venue where the **Gher** dance is performed on a massive scale, attracting thousands of **tourists** and **ethnographers**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Rathwa Ni Gher** involves complex **choreography** where dancers form circles and move in patterns that represent the cosmic order and the **cycle of nature**.
 
• Performers often paint their bodies with **white clay** (limestone) or **Pithora colors**, symbolizing a connection with the divine and the ancestral spirits of the **Rathwa** tribe.
 
• The **Gher** festival is not just a dance but a major social event where **matrimonial alliances** are often initiated, and community bonds are strengthened within the **tribal landscape of India**.
 
• The **Government of India** and the state of **Gujarat** have taken several steps to preserve these **indigenous** art forms under cultural heritage conservation programs.

questions.question: Who led the Khasi resistance against British interference in the 1830s?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tirot Sing**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tirot Sing**, also known as **U Tirot Sing Syiem**, was the chief (Syiem) of **Nongkhlaw** in the **Khasi Hills** of **Meghalaya**. He is celebrated as a hero of the **Khasi** people for leading the resistance against the **British East India Company**. *Hence, option A is correct.*
 
• The conflict, known as the **Anglo-Khasi War**, began in **1829** when the **British** sought to construct a road through the **Khasi Hills** to connect the **Brahmaputra Valley** (Guwahati) with the **Surma Valley** (Sylhet, now in **Bangladesh**).
 
• **Tirot Sing** initially agreed to the road project under the impression it would facilitate trade, but soon realized the **British** intended to establish permanent military outposts and impose taxes, which threatened **Khasi** sovereignty.
 
• In **April 1829**, **Tirot Sing** launched an attack on a **British** party at **Nongkhlaw**, marking the start of a fierce **guerilla warfare** campaign that lasted for four years.
 
• Despite the lack of modern weaponry, the **Khasi** warriors used traditional weapons like bows, arrows, and shields to resist the superior military might of the **British**.
 
• **Tirot Sing** was eventually captured by the **British** in **January 1833** after being betrayed. He was deported to **Dhaka**, where he died in captivity on **17 July 1835**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rani Gaidinliu:**

 
 
• She was a **Naga** spiritual and political leader who led a revolt against **British** rule in **India**.
 
• At the age of **13**, she joined the **Heraka** religious movement led by her cousin **Haiphou Jadonang**.
 
• The movement later turned into a political struggle to drive out the **British** from **Manipur** and the surrounding **Naga** areas.
 
• She was arrested in **1932** at the age of **16** and sentenced to life imprisonment, but was released after **India** gained **Independence** in **1947**.
 
 
 
• **Alluri Sitarama Raju:**
 
 
• He was a revolutionary who led the **Rampa Rebellion** of **1922** in the **Godavari** district of **Andhra Pradesh**.
 
• He mobilized the tribal people against the **1882 Madras Forest Act**, which restricted their free movement in the forest and prevented them from practicing **Podu** (shifting) cultivation.
 
• Raju was highly influenced by the **Non-Cooperation Movement** but believed that **India** could be liberated only by the use of force.
 
• He was captured and executed by the **British** in **1924**.
 
 
 
• **Sidhu Murmu:**
 
 
• **Sidhu Murmu**, along with his brother **Kanhu Murmu**, led the **Santhal Rebellion** (also known as the Santhal Hul) in **1855-56**.
 
• The rebellion took place in the **Santhal Pargana** region of present-day **Jharkhand** and **West Bengal**.
 
• The movement was directed against the **British East India Company** and the **Zamindari** system (landlords) who exploited the **Santhal** tribal people.
 
• The **Santhals** declared **Independence** and established their own administration before the **British** suppressed the movement with extreme violence in **1856**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Khasi** people follow a **matrilineal** system where lineage and inheritance are traced through the mother. This unique social structure has been preserved for centuries in the **Khasi Hills**.
 
• The **State of Meghalaya** celebrates **U Tirot Sing Day** every year on **July 17** to commemorate his sacrifice and bravery.
 
• The **British** expansion in **North-East India** during the **19th century** often led to conflicts with local tribes over land rights, forest resources, and administrative control.
 
• The **Anglo-Khasi War** is significant because it was one of the earliest and most prolonged resistances faced by the **British** in the mountainous regions of **North-East India**.

questions.question: The Golden Quadrilateral connects which of the following cities?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Golden Quadrilateral (GQ)** is a national highway network connecting the four major **metropolitan cities** of India: **Delhi** (North), **Kolkata** (East), **Mumbai** (West), and **Chennai** (South). *Hence, option C is correct.*
 
• It is the **largest highway project** in **India** and the **fifth-longest** highway network in the world, with a total length of approximately **5,846 kilometers** (3,633 miles).
 
• The project was first planned by former Prime Minister **Atal Bihari Vajpayee** in **1999**, and the foundation stone was laid the same year. Construction began in **2001** and the project was officially completed in **January 2012**.
 
• The management and maintenance of the Golden Quadrilateral are handled by the **National Highways Authority of India (NHAI)**, which operates under the **Ministry of Road Transport and Highways**.
 
• Option A mentions Mumbai, Pune, Hyderabad, and Bangalore. While these are key industrial hubs, they do not form the four vertices of the national quadrilateral project. *Hence, option A is incorrect.*
 
• Option B includes Delhi, Bhopal, Ahmedabad, and Mumbai. Although the highway passes through or near some of these areas, Bhopal is not a primary endpoint of the GQ. *Hence, option B is incorrect.*
 
• Option D includes Chennai, Bangalore, Hyderabad, and Kolkata. While the GQ passes through **Bangalore** on the Mumbai-Chennai segment, **Hyderabad** is not one of the four main corners. *Hence, option D is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Components and Routes:**

 
 
• The **Delhi-Kolkata** segment is primarily covered by **NH 19** (formerly NH 2) and **NH 44**.
 
• The **Mumbai-Delhi** segment and **Mumbai-Chennai** segment are parts of the high-traffic **NH 48** (formerly NH 8 and NH 4).
 
• The **Kolkata-Chennai** segment follows the eastern coastline and is designated as **NH 16** (formerly NH 5).
 
 
 
• **Geographic Reach:**
 
 
• The network passes through **13 States** and **Union Territories** in India, including **Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Delhi, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal**.
 
• Major cities located on the network include **Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Bhubaneswar, Jaipur, Kanpur, Pune, Surat, and Vijayawada**.
 
 
 
• **Economic Impact:**
 
 
• The project facilitates faster **transportation** of goods between major **ports** and industrial cities, significantly boosting **GDP growth**.
 
• It has helped in reducing the **travel time** between major metros by **20-30%** and has lowered **fuel consumption** and vehicle wear and tear.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Technical Features:**

 
 
• The highways consist of **four to six lanes** of high-quality paved roads, designed to handle heavy industrial traffic and high-speed passenger vehicles.
 
• It was the **Phase I** of the **National Highways Development Project (NHDP)**, which also includes the **North-South and East-West Corridors**.
 
 
 
• **Comparative Context:**
 
 
• The **North-South Corridor** connects **Srinagar** in Jammu & Kashmir to **Kanyakumari** in Tamil Nadu.
 
• The **East-West Corridor** connects **Silchar** in Assam to **Porbandar** in Gujarat.
 
• The intersection point of these two corridors is **Jhansi** in **Uttar Pradesh**.
 
 
 
• **Project Cost:**
 
 
• The initial estimated cost of the project was around **₹600 billion** (approximately **US$7.2 billion** in current terms), largely funded through **fuel cess** and market borrowings by the **Government of India**.

questions.question: Which characteristic best differentiates Static RAM (SRAM) from Dynamic RAM (DRAM), leading to SRAM being used for CPU cache and DRAM for main system memory (RAM)?

options.text: DRAM is non-volatile, while SRAM is volatile.
SRAM is significantly faster, more expensive, and consumes less power than DRAM.
SRAM requires constant refreshing to hold data, while DRAM does not.
DRAM is located directly on the CPU die, while SRAM is located on the motherboard.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**SRAM is significantly faster, more expensive, and consumes less power than DRAM**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Static Random Access Memory (SRAM)** and **Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM)** are both types of **volatile memory**, meaning they lose stored information when power is removed. However, their internal architecture differs significantly.
 
• **SRAM** uses a complex circuit of **four to six transistors** to store each bit of data, which forms a **flip-flop**. This allows it to maintain data without the need for a **refresh cycle** as long as power is supplied. ***Hence, the characteristic of not needing a refresh makes it faster.***
 
• **DRAM** stores data using a **single transistor** and a **capacitor** for each bit. Since capacitors naturally leak charge, **DRAM** must be **refreshed** thousands of times per **second** to prevent data loss. ***This constant refreshing makes DRAM slower than SRAM.***
 
• Due to the higher number of components (transistors) per bit, **SRAM** is much **less dense** and more **expensive** to manufacture compared to **DRAM**. Consequently, **SRAM** is used in small quantities for **L1, L2, and L3 CPU Cache**, while **DRAM** is used for large-capacity **main system memory (RAM)**.
 
• **SRAM** typically has access speeds in the range of **1 to 10 nanoseconds**, whereas modern **DRAM** usually operates with access times around **60 nanoseconds** or more, depending on the **DDR (Double Data Rate)** generation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure and Functions:**

 
 
• **SRAM:** Because it is placed closer to or directly on the **CPU die**, it reduces the **latency** between the processor and the data it needs to execute instructions. It acts as a high-speed buffer.
 
• **DRAM:** Its **simple design** (one transistor, one capacitor) allows for **billions of cells** to be packed into a single **integrated circuit**, making it possible to have **8GB, 16GB, or 32GB** modules at a consumer-friendly price point.
 
 
 
• **Power Consumption:**
 
 
• **SRAM** is more power-efficient when **idle** because it does not require a refresh current. However, at **high speeds**, its power consumption can increase significantly.
 
• **DRAM** consumes power continuously due to the **refresh cycles** required to maintain the state of the **capacitors**, even when the system is not actively accessing the memory.
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• **SRAM** is used in **routers, printers, LCD screens**, and as **buffer memory** in hard drives, in addition to **CPU Caches**.
 
• **DRAM** is the primary technology for **System RAM** in **personal computers, smartphones, and gaming consoles**. Variations like **VRAM (Video RAM)** are used in **Graphics Processing Units (GPUs)**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Evolution:** **Robert Dennard** at **IBM** invented **DRAM** in **1966**, which revolutionized computing by providing a **low-cost** alternative to earlier magnetic-core memory.
 
• **Volatile vs Non-Volatile:** Both **SRAM** and **DRAM** are **volatile**. This distinguishes them from **Non-Volatile Memory (NVM)** like **Flash Memory (SSD)** or **ROM**, which retain data even after the power is turned off.
 
• **SDRAM (Synchronous DRAM):** Most modern computers use **SDRAM**, which synchronizes itself with the **system clock** to improve efficiency. The current industry standards are **DDR4** and **DDR5**, which offer higher **bandwidth** and lower **voltage** requirements.
 
• **Cost-Performance Trade-off:** If a computer used only **SRAM** for its **16GB** of memory, the machine would be incredibly fast but would cost **thousands of dollars** more and take up significantly more physical space.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements.

1. Lord Mayo’s Resolution of 1870 on financial decentralization visualized the development of local self-government institutions.

2. Hobhouse was the Chairman of the Royal Commission on Decentralization.

3. Under the Government of India Act of 1919, local self-government became a reserved subject.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1 and 2 only**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Lord Mayo’s Resolution of 1870** on **financial decentralization** was a landmark step that aimed to delegate the management of certain local services, such as **education, health, and roads**, to provincial governments. It specifically visualized that this process would encourage the development of **local self-government institutions** by allowing local bodies to manage local needs through local taxation. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• The **Royal Commission on Decentralization** was appointed in **1907** (and submitted its report in **1909**) to investigate the financial and administrative relations between the Government of India, provincial governments, and local bodies. The commission was chaired by **C.E.H. Hobhouse** (Sir Charles Hobhouse), and it recommended that **village panchayats** and local boards should be given more powers and resources. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• Under the **Government of India Act of 1919**, also known as the **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms**, a system of **Dyarchy** was introduced in the provinces. In this system, subjects were divided into **"Reserved"** (managed by the Governor and his Executive Council) and **"Transferred"** (managed by the Governor and Indian Ministers). **Local self-government** was made a **Transferred subject**, meaning it was placed under the charge of an **Indian minister** responsible to the provincial legislature, rather than being a reserved subject. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lord Ripon’s Resolution (1882):** Often hailed as the **"Magna Carta"** of local self-government in India, **Lord Ripon** is known as the **Father of Local Self-Government**. His resolution advocated for the establishment of local boards with a **majority of non-official members** and **elected chairmen** wherever possible, emphasizing that local government should be an instrument of **political and popular education**.
 
• **The Government of India Act, 1935:** This act abolished **Dyarchy** in the provinces and introduced **Provincial Autonomy**. Under this act, **local self-government** continued to be a provincial subject, further strengthening the legislative and executive control of Indian ministers over local bodies and leading to the enactment of various **village panchayat acts** across different provinces.
 
• **Post-Independence Developments:** After **1947**, the importance of local self-government was recognized in the **Directive Principles of State Policy** under **Article 40** of the **Constitution of India**, which mandates the state to organize **village panchayats**. This eventually led to the **73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts of 1992**, which provided constitutional status to **Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)** and **Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)**.
 
• **Dyarchy under the 1919 Act:** The division of subjects into **Reserved** and **Transferred** was a unique feature. While **Transferred subjects** included **Education, Public Health, and Local Self-Government**, the **Reserved subjects** included critical areas like **Police, Justice, Land Revenue, and Finance**, which ensured that the **British Governor** maintained ultimate control over the most powerful departments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Chronology:** The evolution of local bodies moved from **Lord Mayo (1870)** focusing on **financial efficiency**, to **Lord Ripon (1882)** focusing on **political education**, and finally to the **1919 Act** where it became a **democratic responsibility** of Indian ministers.
 
• **Structure of Local Bodies:** Historically, **Municipal Corporations** were established early in **Presidency towns** like **Madras (1688)**, **Bombay (1726)**, and **Calcutta (1726)**. However, organized rural local government only gained momentum after the **Hobhouse Commission** and the **1919 reforms**.
 
• **Financial Decentralization:** Lord Mayo's resolution was significant because it fixed a **fixed grant** for provinces and allowed them to manage local affairs, which was the first practical step towards **administrative decentralization** in British India.

questions.question: Which Sangam text, from the 2nd century CE, is an epic about a chaste wife’s devotion?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Silappatikaram**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Silappatikaram**, meaning "The Tale of an Anklet," is one of the **Five Great Epics** of **Tamil literature**, composed during the **2nd century CE**. Hence, this option is **correct**.
 
• It was written by **Ilango Adigal**, who is believed to be a **Chera prince** and a brother of King **Senguttuvan**. The author eventually became a **Jain monk**.
 
• The epic tells the story of **Kannagi**, a chaste and devoted wife whose husband, **Kovalan**, leaves her for a dancer named **Madhavi**. After losing his wealth, Kovalan returns to Kannagi, and they travel to **Madurai** to start a new life.
 
• The plot reaches its climax when **Kovalan** is wrongfully executed by the **Pandyan King** for allegedly stealing the Queen's anklet. **Kannagi** proves his innocence using her own jewel-filled anklet and, in her fury, burns down the city of **Madurai**.
 
• This work is considered a masterpiece for its **vivid descriptions** of the three major Tamil kingdoms: the **Cholas** (Puhar), the **Pandyas** (Madurai), and the **Cheras** (Vanjikandam).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Manimekalai**:

 
 
• Written by **Sattanar**, this epic is a sequel to **Silappatikaram**. It focuses on the life of **Manimekalai**, the daughter of **Kovalan** and **Madhavi**.
 
• The theme of this text is **renunciation** and the propagation of **Buddhism**. It contains detailed **philosophical** and **logical** debates. Hence, this option is **incorrect** as it focuses on Buddhism rather than the devotion of a wife.
 
 
 
• **Tolkappiyam**:
 
 
• This is the oldest extant work of **Tamil grammar** and poetics, attributed to **Tolkappiyar**.
 
• It provides insights into the **linguistic** structure of Old Tamil and the **socio-economic** conditions of the **Sangam period**. Hence, this option is **incorrect** as it is a grammatical treatise, not an epic poem.
 
 
 
• **Pattuppattu**:
 
 
• Known as the "Ten Idylls," it is an anthology of **ten long poems** that are part of the **Eighteen Greater Texts** (Pathinenmaelkanakku).

__
 
• The **Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)** is a regional intergovernmental organization established to promote **political and social stability** amid rising tensions among the **Asia-Pacific's** post-colonial states.
 
• **India** is a country located in **South Asia** and is not a member of the **ASEAN** bloc, which is specifically for **Southeast Asian** nations. However, **India** is a significant **Strategic Dialogue Partner** of the group. *Hence, statement A is correct as India is NOT a member.*
 
• **Indonesia** is one of the **five founding members** of **ASEAN**. The organization's **Secretariat** is also located in its capital, **Jakarta**. *Hence, statement B is incorrect.*
 
• **Thailand** is a **founding member** of the organization. In fact, the founding document of the bloc is known as the **Bangkok Declaration**, signed in **1967** in **Thailand**. *Hence, statement C is incorrect.*
 
• **Myanmar** officially joined **ASEAN** on **July 23, 1997**. It is one of the **ten permanent members** of the association. *Hence, statement D is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Establishment and History:**

 
 
• **ASEAN** was established on **8 August 1967** in **Bangkok, Thailand**.
 
• The **five original founding fathers** of **ASEAN** were **Indonesia**, **Malaysia**, **Philippines**, **Singapore**, and **Thailand**.
 
• The **ASEAN Declaration** (**Bangkok Declaration**) outlined the organization's goals to accelerate **economic growth** and promote **regional peace**.
 
 
 
• **Membership Evolution:**
 
 
• The current **10 members** are **Brunei** (joined in **1984**), **Vietnam** (**1995**), **Laos** and **Myanmar** (**1997**), and **Cambodia** (**1999**), along with the five founders.
 
• In **November 2022**, **ASEAN** agreed "in principle" to admit **Timor-Leste** as the group's **11th member**.
 
 
 
• **Organizational Structure:**
 
 
• The **ASEAN Summit** is the highest policy-making body, comprising the **Heads of State or Government**.
 
• The **motto** of **ASEAN** is **"One Vision, One Identity, One Community"**.
 
• **August 8th** is observed annually as **ASEAN Day**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **India-ASEAN Relationship:**

 
 
• **India** began its formal engagement with **ASEAN** as a **Sectoral Dialogue Partner** in **1992**.
 
• It graduated to a **Full Dialogue Partner** in **1995** and further to a **Strategic Partner** during the **ASEAN-India Commemorative Summit** in **2012**.
 
• The relationship is a central pillar of **India's Act East Policy**, focusing on **4Cs**: **Commerce**, **Connectivity**, **Culture**, and **Capacity Building**.
 
 
 
• **Regional Forums:**
 
 
• **ASEAN Plus Three:** This forum includes the 10 **ASEAN** members plus **China**, **Japan**, and **South Korea**.
 
• **East Asia Summit (EAS):** A premier forum for strategic dialogue, where **India**, **the United States**, and **Russia** participate alongside **ASEAN** members.
 
• **ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF):** Established in **1994** to facilitate dialogue on **security issues** in the **Indo-Pacific** region.

questions.question: The Bhabar and Terai regions of the Great Indian Plains differ primarily in:

options.text: Permeability of soil and groundwater availability

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Permeability of soil and groundwater availability**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Bhabar** and **Terai** are distinct physiological divisions of the **Great Indian Plains** located at the foothills of the **Himalayas**. Their primary difference lies in the **geological composition** and the resulting **permeability of the soil**.
 
• **Bhabar** region consists of **porous** rock debris and **pebbles** brought down by rivers from the **Shiwalik** ranges. Due to this high **porosity** and **permeability**, small streams and rivers often disappear underground when they enter this belt. ***Hence, statement A is correct as it highlights the core physical difference.***
 
• **Terai** region is situated to the **south** of the **Bhabar**. In this zone, the underground streams of the **Bhabar** belt re-emerge at the surface, creating a **marshy** and **swampy** tract. The soil here is **silty** and less permeable than Bhabar, leading to high **groundwater availability** and water-logging.
 
• Regarding **Rainfall** and **wind direction**, both regions are part of the same latitudinal belt and generally experience similar **monsoonal** patterns, though **Terai** receives slightly more effective moisture due to its water-retention capacity. ***Hence, statement B is not the primary difference.***
 
• Both regions are fundamentally **influenced by the Himalayan Rivers** such as the **Ganga**, **Yamuna**, and **Brahmaputra**, as they are formed by their **alluvial deposits**. ***Hence, statement C is a similarity rather than a difference.***
 
• While **human settlement patterns** differ (with **Terai** being more intensely cultivated for **Sugarcane** and **Rice** after forest clearing), this is a **consequence** of the physical differences rather than the primary geographical cause. ***Hence, statement D is a secondary factor.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Bhabar Belt:**

 
 
• **Location:** It stretches from the **Indus** river in the **West** to the **Tista** river in the **East**. It runs parallel to the **Shiwaliks**.
 
• **Features:** The width of this belt varies between **8 km to 16 km**. It is characterized by **un-assorted sediments**.
 
• **Uses:** It is generally **unsuitable for agriculture** because of the massive presence of **boulders** and **pebbles**, though big trees with deep roots can thrive here.
 
 
 
• **The Terai Belt:**
 
 
• **Location:** It lies south of the **Bhabar** belt.
 
• **Features:** Its width is approximately **10 km to 20 km**. It was traditionally a **thickly forested** region with rich **wildlife**.
 
• **Development:** After **1947**, many forests in the **Terai** of **Uttar Pradesh** and **Uttarakhand** were cleared to settle migrants and for **agricultural expansion**.
 
• **Functions:** It serves as a natural **reservoir** for groundwater and is highly **productive** for crops like **Wheat**, **Rice**, and **Sugarcane**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Great Indian Plains** are also divided into **Bhangar** and **Khadar** regions based on the **age** of the **alluvium**.
 
• **Bhangar:** This is the **older alluvium** of the plains and forms the **upland** terraces. It contains **calcareous deposits** locally known as **Kankar**. It is less fertile compared to **Khadar**.
 
• **Khadar:** This represents the **new alluvium** deposited by **floods** almost every **year**. It is very **fertile** and is ideal for **intensive agriculture**.
 
• **Geographical Data:** The total **length** of the **Great Indian Plains** is about **2,400 km**, and its **width** varies from **150 km to 300 km**.
 
• The formation of these plains is attributed to the **filling of a deep depression** (foredeep) between the **Himalayas** and the **Peninsular Plateau** during the **Pleistocene period**.

questions.question: What will be the positive difference in the population of a town 3 years ago and 2 years ago, if its current population is 450000 and the population has been increasing at a rate of 25% every year?

Growth factor = 1.25

2 yrs ago = 450000 ÷ (1.25)² = 450000 ÷ 1.5625 = 288000

3 yrs ago = 288000 ÷ 1.25 = 230400

Difference = 288000 − 230400 = 57600

**∴ Answer = 57,600**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

Current population = 450000

Growth rate = 25% per year

**Formula used:**

Past population = Present ÷ (1 + r/100)ⁿ

**Calculation:**

⇒ Population 2 years ago = 450000 ÷ (1.25)²

⇒ = 450000 ÷ 1.5625 = 288000

⇒ Population 3 years ago = 450000 ÷ (1.25)³

⇒ = 450000 ÷ 1.953125 = 230400

⇒ Difference = 288000 − 230400 = 57600

**∴ The correct answer is 57,600.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Population Formula

P = P₀ × (1 + r/100)ⁿ

Reverse Growth

Past value = Present ÷ growth factor

Successive Growth

Each year multiplies by same factor (1.25 here)

Divide step-by-step instead of using powers for easier calculation
